questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript and how does it work?
questions.title: Closures Javascript
questions.direct_answer: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the captured variables stay alive (and writable) after the outer function returns. Closures give functions private, persistent state.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the captured variables stay alive (and writable) after the outer function returns. Closures give functions private, persistent state.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The canonical example, verified:

```js
function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;             // captured by the inner function
  return () => {
    count++;                  // reads and WRITES the captured count
    return count;
  };
}

const counter = makeCounter(); // makeCounter returned, count SURVIVED
console.log(counter());  // 1 — the closure holds count
console.log(counter();  // 2 — same variable, incremented
console.log(counter());  // 3 — state persists
```

A closure IS: the function + the captured lexical environment. makeCounter returned long ago, but count didn't die — the inner function's reference keeps it alive, and the SAME variable is read and written across every call.

The everyday closures (you write them constantly):
1. Callbacks that reference outer variables — every event handler, every Promise.then
2. Module pattern — private state hidden inside the closure
3. Partial application / currying — (a) => (b) => a + b — the inner function closes over a
4. Memoization — the cache captured by the function

The loop-variable capture (THE classic interview question): a closure in a loop captures the VARIABLE, not the value. Pre-let, var i was ONE variable shared across iterations — all closures saw the final value. let i creates a NEW binding per iteration — each closure captures its own.

The memory note (the practical angle interviewers appreciate): a closure keeps its captured variables alive as long as the closure itself is reachable — closures over large data are a leak pattern (capture the one string you need, not the whole request object).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M[makeCounter: count = 0] --> I[returns arrow fn]
    I -.->|captures| M
    M --> V[count stays alive — closure holds it]
    C[calls: counter] --> I
    I --> R[count++ — reads and writes the SAME count]
    V --> P[persists across calls — 1, 2, 3]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanism, precisely: when a function is CREATED (not called), it receives a hidden [[Environment]] reference to the lexical environment where it was defined. When the function is CALLED later (even after the outer scope returned), its variable lookup chain starts from the captured [[Environment]] — the outer variables are found and alive because the closure's reference kept the environment from being garbage-collected.

The per-iteration let mechanics (the loop question's deep answer): each for-let iteration creates a NEW environment that copies the current value of i into a FRESH binding. Each closure captures its OWN environment's i — which the engine then keeps alive per closure. With var, all closures captured the SAME function-level environment — all seeing the same i, which finished the loop before any callback ran.

The IIFE pre-let fix (the historical pattern): (function(i) { callbacks.push(() => i) })(i) — the immediately-invoked function created a new scope per iteration, passing the VALUE as a parameter (a new binding per call). let made this obsolete.

The V8 optimization reality: the engine analyzes which captured variables are actually USED and captures only those (the scope's 'context' allocation is minimal) — a closure that only uses 'a' from a scope with 10 variables carries only a's environment. The naive model (the whole scope hoisted) is wrong; the engine is surgical.
